card: Good news: in the plural, gender almost stops mattering. Dative **-ам/-ям**, instrumental **-ами/-ями**, prepositional **-ах/-ях** are the same for every noun: **кни́гам, кни́гами, кни́гах**; **стола́м, стола́ми, стола́х**. Only the nominative and genitive vary, and the accusative copies one of them (animate = genitive).

sections.body: Over centuries, Russian merged its plural declensions into one. The three "oblique" plural cases (dative, instrumental, prepositional) are now identical across all genders, which makes the plural much easier than the singular once you have the nominative and genitive.

table.caption: A few nouns keep an old instrumental in **-ьми**: **детьми́**, **людьми́**, and the optional **дверьми́**.

sections.title: The accusative in the plural
sections.body:
For **all** genders, the plural accusative copies the nominative for things and the genitive for living beings:

- **Я ви́жу столы́ / кни́ги / о́кна.** (inanimate: = nominative)
- **Я ви́жу студе́нтов / де́вушек / дете́й.** (animate: = genitive)

In the singular this applied only to masculine nouns; in the plural it covers feminine and neuter animals and people too: **Я люблю́ ко́шек.**

sections.title: Stress in the plural
sections.body: Many common nouns move their stress in the plural, usually to the ending: **го́род → города́, городо́в**; **сло́во → слова́**; **окно́ → о́кна** (the other way). The plural stress is usually the same in all plural cases, apart from the nominative and accusative. Check the word page when in doubt; the lab tables show every form.

English has one plural form (*tables*) plus *'s* (*tables'*). Russian has six, but four of them follow one pattern across all nouns, so the real work is just the nominative and genitive plural you already know.

examples.en: There are many museums in these cities.
